description.narrative: Programmet syftar till att främja medborgarnas (särskilt marginaliserade samhällens) egenmakt och fria deltagande i styrnings- och utvecklingsprocesser genom att få tillgång till relevant, tillförlitlig, inkluderande information och medieinnehåll.

The programme seeks to promote the empowerment and free participation of citizens (particularly marginalized communities) in governance and development processes, through accessing relevant, reliable, inclusive information and media content.

The overall objective: Zimbabwean citizens (particularly marginalised communities) freely participate in, and contribute to, governance and development processes.
Specific objective: Zimbabwean citizens (particularly marginalised communities) are informed and empowered with relevant, reliable, inclusive information and media content enabling meaningful participation in development and governance processes.
Outcome 1: Communities, especially marginalised and special interest groups access and use credible information to participate in public debate on developmental and governance issues
Outcome 2: Professional, reliable, innovative, sustainable comprehensive media enable informed citizen agency and engagement with a focus on marginalised communities
Outcome 3: Relevant duty-bearers ensure a conducive media policy and operational environments enabling safe journalistic practice and citizens participation

sector.narrative: Media and free flow of information

description.narrative:
The Media Development Programme in Zimbabwe represents a significant initiative to enhance media freedom, journalist safety, and public access to information within a complex political and institutional landscape. Implemented through a collaborative, multi-stakeholder approach, the programme reached all ten provinces and engaged a wide range of actors, including civil society organisations, training institutions, and community-based groups. This inclusive strategy contributed to a more representative media environment, with notable achievements such as a 62.5% reduction in media freedom violations during the 2023 elections compared to 2018, and the accreditation of 60 women among 140 community radio reporters.
The programme supported the licensing of 14 community radio stations, some of which began generating revenue through government-approved advertisingan important step toward sustainability. In parallel, over 1,200 journalists and media workers were trained in ethical journalism, digital security, and investigative reporting, ensuring broad geographic and demographic coverage. Additionally, more than 300 community dialogues were held to promote media literacy and raise awareness of the Freedom of Information Act, helping bridge the gap between media institutions and the communities they serve.
Digital transformation was another key focus, with the digitisation of 12 community radio stations significantly improving broadcast quality and reach. Youth engagement also saw success, with around 500 young media practitioners participating in internships, fellowships, and campus radio initiativesefforts that nurtured emerging talent and diversified media voices.
Legal support was provided in over 80 cases involving media freedom violations, contributing to a 40% increase in successful legal outcomes for journalists. Furthermore, more than 1,500 hours of community radio content were produced, covering critical topics such as local governance, health, education, and gender issuesstrengthening informed civic participation.
Despite these achievements, the programme revealed several weaknesses, particularly within the implementing agency, International Media Support (IMS). A major concern was IMSs failure to meet reporting deadlines. Reports were often delayed, lacked clarity, and failed to present a coherent narrative of the programmes impact. These communication lapses, compounded by the absence of quality-checked data, created confusion about the programmes objectives and progress. For example, only 204 of the targeted 312 fact-checked articles were completeda 34.6% shortfallhighlighting the need for a robust data collection and monitoring system.
Gender inclusivity, while promoted, lacked adequate safeguards for women journalists. Alarmingly, 73.4% reported verbal sexual harassment, 29% experienced physical harassment, and 64.86% felt unsafe at work. Yet, only 15.15% of victims reported these incidents, indicating a lack of trust in institutional support mechanisms.
Resource allocation and technical support were uneven. While some community radio stations benefited from licensing and advertising revenue, many struggled with outdated equipment, limited technical expertise, and unreliable power supply. These disparities undermined the programmes goal of equitable media access. Additionally, heavy reliance on unpaid volunteers led to high turnover and inconsistent content production. Although revenue-generation mechanisms were introduced, they were not scaled effectively to ensure long-term sustainability.
Collaborations with institutions such as Fojo Media Institute and Great Zimbabwe University contributed significantly to training and capacity-building. However, the absence of a unified strategic framework occasionally compromised the programmes coherence and effectiveness. IMSs approach to emerging challenges was often reactive rather than proactive. While overt violations were reduced, sporadic instances of harassment and surveillance persisted, underscoring the need for more comprehensive protective mechanisms.
In conclusion, the Media Development Programme in Zimbabwe made commendable progress in a difficult environment. Its achievements reflect the dedication of all involved. However, to fully realise its potential and ensure lasting impact, there is a clear need to strengthen internal systems, deepen stakeholder engagement, and adopt a more proactive and inclusive approach. By addressing these areas, IMS can advance its vision of a transparent, inclusive, and democratic media landscape in Zimbabwe.
